questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A headline and what it foregrounds
questions.learningObjective: say what a headline puts at the centre and what it leaves out
questions.stem: A news site runs the headline 'Tres años sin agua: el pueblo que se quedó sin fuente'. What has that headline chosen to foreground?

options.text: The length of the drought and the loss of the village's own water supply
The cost of repairing the pumping station in the centre of the village
options.misconception: imports a repair bill the headline never mentions into the story it names

options.text: The dispute between the regional government and the farmers of the area
options.misconception: reads a political conflict into a headline about a water shortage

options.text: The decision to move the village's inhabitants to another settlement
options.misconception: assumes a headline about losing water is really announcing a relocation

questions.explanation: A headline works by choosing one part of the story to put first and letting the rest wait for the text. Here the framing colon splits the piece into a measure and a consequence: three years without rain, and a town left without its spring. Those are the only two things the wording supplies, so they are the two things the headline is foregrounding. A reader who looks for a repair bill, a political quarrel or a relocation has added material from elsewhere, which is exactly the habit a headline rewards and a careful reader has to resist. The number is the part worth noticing as well, because a precise figure in a headline is usually chosen for the shock it delivers rather than for how much it explains.
questions.hint: Ask which nouns and which figure actually appear in the headline, and ignore the rest.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An advertisement and its target audience
questions.learningObjective: read the audience an advertisement is built for out of its images
questions.stem: A poster shows a young family eating breakfast at a table, under the words 'Empieza bien cada mañana'. Who is that poster built for?

options.text: Households with children, since the family makes the product a daily habit to keep
People who eat out, since the table shown is furnished as a restaurant table
options.misconception: reads a domestic tablecloth and a sideboard as the fittings of an eating house

options.text: Single workers, since a family at a table is the morning that they do not have
options.misconception: takes the household shown as the audience the advertisement is excluding

options.text: Anyone at all, since the wording names no audience and therefore cannot exclude one
options.misconception: believes an advertisement reaches only the people it names in words

questions.explanation: An advertisement does not have to name its audience, because the picture does the work. A family at a breakfast table is a household with a child in it, and the slogan starts bien cada mañana, which is the language of repetition rather than of indulgence: the advertiser wants a habit, not a treat. A single person eating alone at a table would have signalled a different market, and a restaurant setting would have signalled another entirely, so the images are the targeting. The claim that an unnamed audience is a general audience confuses what is written with who is shown, and it is worth noticing that a poster aimed at a household says nothing about age, which is why the choice of the scene rather than the slogan is the thing to study.
questions.hint: Ask who is sitting at the table, and whether the slogan is about a habit or an occasion.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A social media post and the brevity it imposes
questions.learningObjective: work out what a very short post leaves for the reader to supply
questions.stem: A post reads 'Uno de estos tres dedos es mentira' beside a photograph of three hands, with no further comment. What does that brevity require of the reader?

options.text: That the reader supply the claim, since the post itself states nothing about the hands
That the reader ignore the picture, since a photograph cannot support a claim at all
options.misconception: assumes an image is worthless as evidence, which overcorrects the opposite error

options.text: That the reader read agreement into the silence, since an unchallenged post is settled
options.misconception: treats the absence of any comment as a comment nobody has made

options.text: That the reader pass it on at once, since a short post is built to travel before it is read
options.misconception: takes the aim of travelling fast as an instruction to the reader rather than a design aim

questions.explanation: A post that short has spent its words on the part that travels and has left the rest to whoever opens it, and what is missing here is the claim: nothing in the three hands or the caption says why one of them is a lie, or what that lie is about. A reader who assumes the silence means agreement is doing the opposite, since the silence is where the argument should have been. The belief that a photograph settles a matter is also worth unlearning, because an image can be cropped and staged and a caption can be wrong about it. Brevity in this form is not a courtesy to the reader's time; it is a way of moving material that cannot be checked quickly.
questions.hint: Ask what the post asserts, as opposed to what it merely shows.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An influencer and the disclosure that applies
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a disclosure meets the standard of being visible
questions.stem: A poster carries a paid advertisement for a skin cream, marked with the single small word 'colaboración' at the foot of the picture. What has that marker done about disclosure?

options.text: It names the commercial link, though it discharges the duty only if a reader can see it
It removes the need for disclosure, because a paid post needs no further mark once labelled
options.misconception: treats any label as the whole of the duty rather than as its beginning

options.text: It proves that money changed hands, which is a fact about the contract and not about readers
options.misconception: reads a disclosure duty as though it were an obligation to record a payment

options.text: It passes the duty to the reader, since a small label is still a label once it is printed
options.misconception: believes that a label buried in the image counts for anyone who never finds it

questions.explanation: A disclosure has to do two jobs at once, and this marker only manages one of them. It names the relationship, which tells an attentive reader that the praise is not independent. It does not reach a reader who never finds it, and a single word set small at the foot of a picture is the classic way to satisfy the letter of a rule while defeating its purpose, because a disclosure that nobody sees has informed nobody. The second option mistakes the label for the whole duty, the third confuses disclosure with a receipt, and the fourth gives the reader the job the poster should have done. The standard is visibility in the same place and at the same scale as the claim.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader who has not noticed the word has in fact been told anything.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An online review and its reliability
questions.learningObjective: weigh a single unverified account as evidence about a business
questions.stem: A restaurant page carries one review, from a reader who writes 'Comí aquí la semana pasada y el arroz estaba excellent'. What is weak about that review as evidence?

options.text: It is a single unverified account with no detail a reader could check against it
It is written by a customer, and only customers ever report on a restaurant
options.misconception: makes the author's identity a virtue when the question is the evidence given

options.text: It is recent, and a recent account is by definition better than an older one
options.misconception: assumes recency settles reliability, which is a claim about time and not about proof

options.text: It is positive, and a positive opinion can never count as evidence of anything
options.misconception: dismisses a favourable report as though its tone cancelled its content

questions.explanation: A review is evidence of one thing, which is that one person reports having eaten there once, and the report here adds a single evaluative word about one dish. There is no second account, no bill, no date beyond a week and no detail a reader could test, so the review can be true and still be a poor basis for a decision. The three distractors are all moves that would make the reader careless in a different direction. Praising the author for being a customer rewards the wrong criterion, since an inspector would count for more. Recency and positivity are not evidence either way, and treating a friendly tone as disqualifying is as unthinking as treating it as proof.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could check in the review besides the word excellent.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A news report and its sourcing
questions.learningObjective: tell attribution to a named body from a route to verification
questions.stem: A report writes 'Según el informe de la asociación, el año 2024 cerró con menos visitors', naming the association but printing no reference. What has the report done about sourcing?

options.text: It attributed the claim to a named body, which is attribution without a route to checking it
It left the claim unattributed, since según is a rhetorical flourish with no naming in it
options.misconception: reads según as decoration when it is the standard marker of a reported source

options.text: It sourced the claim completely, since naming a body discharges every requirement there is
options.misconception: believes a name is a source, overlooking that the report cannot be found

options.text: It removed the reporter's own responsibility, since no one is named as the author of the figures
options.misconception: takes a shift of blame onto a body as though it released the journalist from duty

questions.explanation: Attribution and verification are two different things and the report has done the first without the second. Según names the body the claim comes from, which tells a reader whose figures these are and therefore whose mistake they would be, and that is a genuine improvement on a bare assertion. But a name is not a source unless it can be reached, and an association a reader has never heard of, with no report to look up and no date for the data, is a name rather than a citation. The distractors fail in three different ways: denying that según attributes anything, treating a name as though it were the report itself, and assuming that shifting responsibility to a body lets the journalist off.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reader could find and read the document the claim is said to come from.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A fact-check and what it verifies
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of a verdict on a claim
questions.stem: A fact-check page is headed 'FALSO' and notes that the claim was first made in 2019 by an account with eleven followers. What has that check established?

options.text: That the claim is unsupported, and not that the opposite statement is itself true
That the opposite statement is true, which a verdict on the claim by itself supplies
options.misconception: reads a finding against a claim as though it were a positive finding for its opposite

options.text: That no one believes the claim, which the age of it and its origin together settle
options.misconception: equates the weakness of a claim's origin with the number of people who accept it

options.text: That the account has been closed, since a verdict carries the power to remove a source
options.misconception: assumes that finding against a claim obliges a platform to delete the account that made it

questions.explanation: A verdict of false is a statement about one claim, and what it establishes is that the claim is not supported, not that some other claim is. That gap is the most useful thing a fact-check teaches, because a reader who thinks a check settles the whole question will stop looking and will sometimes settle on a story that has no more support than the one that was checked. The evidence given here is well chosen for that purpose: a first post from 2019 and an account with eleven followers show that the claim was circulating early and from a source with no standing, which is a reason to doubt it. Belief is a separate matter, since a false claim can be widely believed, and removal is a platform decision rather than an outcome of checking.
questions.hint: Ask what the verdict is about, and refuse to let it stand for anything wider.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An algorithm and the ranking it produces
questions.learningObjective: predict the order a stated ranking rule will produce
questions.stem: A feed says that results are ordered by 'the interaction each item has had so far'. Which order does that rule produce?

options.text: Items people have already reacted to come first, whatever their relation to the reader
Items whose words match the search come first, because words outrank reactions here
options.misconception: assumes a stated rule about reactions is really a rule about matching words

options.text: Items that are newest come first, since a new item has had no reactions to weigh
options.misconception: replaces a cumulative measure with a date, which the rule never mentions

options.text: Items that cost the platform most come first, because the order follows what pays
options.misconception: supplies a motive the stated rule does not contain, however plausible it is

questions.explanation: A ranking rule has to be read as a rule and not as an intention. Interaction is a count of what people have already done, so the rule rewards whatever has drawn a reaction, and it cannot tell whether that reaction was approval or a pause caused by indignation. The relation of an item to the reader is not in the rule at all, which is the practical consequence a reader should take away: a feed ordered this way will keep showing what has already worked, whether or not it is what was asked for. The distractors each import something the sentence does not contain, whether word matching, recency or payment, and each of those is a real thing a platform may do, which is exactly why the rule has to be read closely.
questions.hint: Take the rule literally and ask what quantity it counts, then predict the order it forces.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A livestream and its interaction model
questions.learningObjective: describe the queue a livestream host works through
questions.stem: A host reads a question aloud from a list that keeps filling while he talks, then answers it and moves to the next. Which interaction model is that?

options.text: A broadcast to many that the audience fills with questions the host drains in turn
A private exchange in which only the people who paid may put a question to the host
options.misconception: assumes access to a broadcast is rationed by money, which the queue contradicts

options.text: A round in which every viewer speaks at once and the host arbitrates the noise
options.misconception: turns an orderly queue into simultaneous speech nobody could follow

options.text: A deferred exchange, since the answers reach each asker privately after the event
options.misconception: reads a live queue as though the replies were sent to individuals later

questions.explanation: The list is the whole model. One voice is heard by many, and the audience cannot speak, so it writes; the host reads what has arrived, answers it aloud for everyone, and moves on, which makes the exchange one to many in delivery and two-way in content. The queue is also why the host chooses the order rather than taking the questions in the order they came, which is the only part of the format that any audience member can influence. The second option would be a paid session, the third a conversation nobody could follow, and the fourth a correspondence, and each is a different product from the one described even though all four use the word live in marketing.
questions.hint: Ask who can speak, who can write, and what the host is working through.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A screen-time report and what it measures
questions.learningObjective: say what a duration figure on a device actually counts
questions.stem: A screen-time report gives 'four hours and twelve minutes' for one day, broken down by app. What is that figure a measure of?

options.text: Time the app was in front of the device, and not what the user was doing inside it
Time spent productively, which the device can judge from the category of the app
options.misconception: credits the device with a judgement about value that it has no way to make

options.text: Notifications delivered, which the system converts into an estimate of minutes
options.misconception: reinterprets a duration as a count that a report of minutes cannot be

options.text: Battery spent by the app, which the system reports as an equivalent duration
options.misconception: supposes a figure in hours and minutes is a substitute for a power reading

questions.explanation: A device can see when its screen is on and which app has the foreground, so that is what a figure in hours and minutes records, and it records nothing about attention. An hour spent reading a long article and an hour spent looking at the same page without reading it are identical in the report, which is the single most important limitation of the number and the reason it is worth looking at the breakdown rather than the total. The second option asks the device to have an opinion it cannot form, since categories are assigned by whoever published the app. The third and fourth read a duration as something it does not measure at all, and a report that offered either would be reporting a different instrument.
questions.hint: Ask what a device can observe about a person and what it has no access to.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A recommendation feed and the signal it optimises for
questions.learningObjective: name the quantity a recommendation system is built to raise
questions.stem: A feed is described as optimising for the time people spend watching. Which quantity is that?

options.text: Watch time, which the system raises and which rewards anything that holds a viewer
Accuracy, which the system checks before any recommendation is allowed to appear
options.misconception: credits a ranking system with a truth test it was never described as running

options.text: Popularity, which the system reads from a public count that sits under each item
options.misconception: confuses a private measure of time with a public tally of approval

options.text: Recency, which the system fixes so that nothing in the feed is ever a day old
options.misconception: replaces a measure of time spent with a measure of age, which is not the same

questions.explanation: Optimising for a quantity means raising that quantity, so a system told to raise the time people spend watching will learn to put in front of them whatever holds them there, and it has no way to tell a satisfying hour from a puzzling one. That single fact explains most of the behaviour people complain about, and it is worth stating in advance rather than discovering. Accuracy and popularity are different quantities that a system may measure for other purposes, and recency is a fourth: none of them is what the sentence says. The useful habit is to ask of any ranking system what it is rewarded for, because the answer is a statement about behaviour rather than about quality.
questions.hint: Take the phrase literally and ask what number would go up if the system succeeded.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A filter bubble and the mechanism that forms it
questions.learningObjective: state the loop by which a filter bubble narrows what a reader sees
questions.stem: What is the mechanism that forms a filter bubble around a reader?

options.text: What a person engages with comes back to them as what they are likely to engage with again
Sites are sorted by country, so a reader is shown the material of the nation they live in
options.misconception: blames geography, which widens a bubble instead of closing it around one person

options.text: Advertisers pick the audience, and the audience is left to choose from what has been funded
options.misconception: explains a bubble by money, which is a different narrowing and often a visible one

options.text: Engines drop duplicates, and a narrow topic leaves few distinct results to show
options.misconception: attributes a personal narrowing to a search engine that was asked for it

questions.explanation: A filter bubble needs a feedback loop, and the loop is this: the material a person opens or finishes or argues with is the evidence the system uses to decide what to show next, so the reader's own habits become the filter. Nothing has to conspire, and no one has to decide to restrict the reader; the narrowing is a by-product of a system doing exactly what it was built to do. Geography and funding narrow what a person can see as well, and both are real, but both are visible to the reader and both are shared with everyone else in the same place. A bubble is narrower than either of those, because it is built from one person's reactions, which is why two people on the same network can be living in quite different feeds.
questions.hint: Ask where the evidence used to choose the next item actually comes from.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A meme and how it transmits
questions.learningObjective: explain what a meme loses when the caption travels alone
questions.stem: A meme's caption makes no sense without a picture the reader has already seen. How does that shape the way a meme spreads?

options.text: It travels in fragments, since a caption separated from the picture loses what it referred to
It travels whole, since the platform carries the picture along with the caption always
options.misconception: assumes every route of transmission preserves the pairing the format needs

options.text: It cannot travel, since a reader without the picture has no way to look it up
options.misconception: overcorrects, since a meme is often found through a reference even when unseen

options.text: It spreads slowly, since the explanation takes more words than the caption has room for
options.misconception: supposes the barrier is space, when the caption is short by design already

questions.explanation: A caption is an index rather than a description: it points at a picture, and a picture that is not there leaves the pointing at nothing. So when a meme travels by a route that keeps only the words, which is a screenshot of the text, a quotation or a spoken retelling, the meaning does not survive intact and the reader either misses the joke or invents one. This is why memes spread unevenly: the image and the words travel together easily, and apart badly. The belief that a platform always carries the pair along confuses one route of sharing with all of them, and the belief that the pair cannot travel at all confuses loss of meaning with impossibility, since a shared reference is often enough for a reader who already has it.
questions.hint: Ask which half of the pair carries the meaning, and what happens when the other half is dropped.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A hashtag and the work it does
questions.learningObjective: say how a hashtag attaches a post to a searchable set
questions.stem: Someone writes #SendasDeAndalucia under a photograph of a footpath. What work is the word with the sign doing?

options.text: It attaches the picture to a set others can find, which is how one post joins a category
It fixes how the caption is spelled, so a reader cannot misread what was written
options.misconception: reads a search label as though it corrected the spelling of the words

options.text: It signs the post as the work of the writer, which a caption alone has no power to do
options.misconception: confuses a topic label with an author credit, which is a different convention

options.text: It shortens the caption, standing in for the words a longer caption would have used
options.misconception: supposes the word is a shortener rather than an address that can be looked up

questions.explanation: A hashtag is an address. Once a post carries one, a person searching for that phrase can find it, which is the only thing the word does, and it is a great deal: it is how a single post becomes part of a set that did not exist before it was posted. It says nothing about spelling, since a typo inside the phrase makes a different address, and it is not a signature, since authorship is established by the account. The belief that it shortens the caption is a reasonable guess from English, where a word prefixed with a sign is read as a label rather than as a link, but the effect is the opposite of shortening: the words stay in the caption and the sign adds a route of access to them. The number of meanings a single post ends up with is the practical measure of it.
questions.hint: Ask what a person could do with that word which the caption alone would not allow.

questions.topic: A podcast and the conventions of the form
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a spoken series a podcast rather than a broadcast
questions.stem: A series of spoken audio episodes is released on a feed without a schedule or a transmitter. Which convention belongs to that form?

A panel speaks at once, so a listener chooses which of several voices to follow
options.misconception: borrows the sound of a roundtable to describe a single voice reading aloud

options.text: A script is read word for word from a page, with no spoken opening of any kind
options.misconception: confuses a disciplined format with one that forbids any spoken framing

options.text: An audience replies inside the recording, so the hosts answer questions as they come
options.misconception: puts live audience voices into a format that is distributed after recording

A listener chooses when to start, chooses which episode, and often listens to part of one while doing something else, which is why each episode has to work alone and why the host establishes who is speaking and what the episode is in the opening moments. The second and fourth options describe something live and simultaneous, which is a different product because the listener cannot ask anything while it plays. The third describes a discipline the form does not demand, since a host who reads aloud without introducing the episode leaves a listener arriving late with no idea what they have joined.
questions.hint: Ask what a listener who arrived late or out of order would need the episode to provide.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A video call and the constraint of delay
questions.learningObjective: name the limit that makes conversation on a video call work differently
questions.stem: A call becomes awkward as the gap between a gesture and its picture grows. Which constraint has the speaker run into?

options.text: Round-trip delay, which imposes a turn-taking rhythm the speakers have to relearn
Screen resolution, which falls as more of the picture is sent over the same connection
options.misconception: picks a quality setting, which alters the image and not the rhythm of a conversation

options.text: Echo removal, which strips the return of a speaker's own voice out of the signal
options.misconception: confuses a fault heard by others with the delay a speaker feels in the round trip

options.text: Colour depth, which is lowered so that a compressed frame can still be displayed
options.misconception: chooses a second quality setting where the complaint was about waiting for a reply

questions.explanation: The symptom described is a gap in time, and a gap in time is delay: a signal goes out, travels, comes back, and is played out, and the sum of that is what the two people are each reacting to. In a room, a speaker interrupts and the other stops, because the two are close enough in time for that to work; at a second or more of delay the same interruption arrives after the other person has finished the thought, and people learn to wait, which is why a call with a long delay feels strangely formal. The other three options are all about the picture and about quality settings, and a call can have a poor picture and a good conversation, which is the clearest evidence that the two are not the same constraint.
questions.hint: Ask whether the complaint is about what is seen or about how long a reply takes to come back.

questions.learningObjective: name a component of digital literacy rather than an adjacent skill
questions.stem: Which of these is a component of digital literacy as the term is normally used?

options.misconception: confuses fluency of operation with judgement about what is read

options.text: Repairing a device by fitting new parts, which is technical work rather than literacy

options.text: Memorising the terms of service of a platform, which the term never asks of anyone

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A strong password and why length beats complexity
questions.learningObjective: explain why a passphrase resists guessing better than a short string
questions.stem: Why does a long passphrase usually resist guessing better than a short string of complicated characters?

options.text: Length multiplies the number of guesses, while a symbol adds only a few at each position
Length counts for nothing, since no attack ever guesses one character at a time
options.misconception: denies the one step at a time guessing that makes a long password hard

options.text: Symbols are counted as several characters, so they scale faster than letters do
options.misconception: assumes a wider alphabet multiplies the space faster than more positions do

options.text: Length helps only when it is short, since a long phrase is harder to keep in mind
options.misconception: reverses the two effects, making a long phrase the weaker of the two options

questions.explanation: The number of keys a guess has to try multiplies with every position added, so a passphrase of ordinary words is astronomically harder to exhaust than a short string, even though each position offers only ordinary letters. Adding symbols helps, because it widens the alphabet at each position, but it widens it by a factor rather than multiplying the whole space, and it costs the user a great deal of effort and errors. The second option is simply false about how guesses are made. The third mistakes a factor for a multiplier, which is the most common miscalculation in the whole area. The fourth has it backwards: a long phrase is easier to remember than a short string of symbols, which is the whole reason it survives being used.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the size of the search space as one more position is added.

questions.topic: Why length beats complexity in a password

answer.exemplar: The size of the space an attacker has to search multiplies with every position added, so four ordinary words put a search of a size no machine finishes, while eight mixed characters put a search a good machine finishes in hours. A symbol does help, and the reason it helps less is that it widens the alphabet at each position rather than multiplying the whole space, which is a factor where a position is a multiplier. The other half of the answer is human: a passphrase of words is typed correctly and remembered, and a string of symbols is neither, and a password that is reset every fortnight because nobody can recall it has a small search space in practice whatever its size on paper. The mistake to name is treating a factor as a multiplier, since a hundred symbols and thirty letters is a few times more work and twenty extra characters is a million times more.

It also has to name the human half, which is the part that decides the outcome in practice: a password that is reset is worse than a weak one, since resetting teaches a user to choose something memorable and short. The last part is worth including for a class, because the difference between a factor and a multiplier is a piece of arithmetic that transfers, and it is the point on which most confident wrong answers about this are built.

questions.topic: What a filter bubble does to a reader's news

answer.exemplar: A filter bubble narrows the range of what a person is shown, not by removing anything but by never proposing it. The mechanism is a loop: the material a reader opens, finishes or argues with is the evidence the system uses to choose the next item, so after a few weeks the feed is largely a record of what the reader has already revealed, and the reader comes to read the feed as though it were the world. The reason two people on the same service see different things is that the input is per person: the same system, the same news, two different sets of reactions, and no disagreement between the two feeds is visible from inside either. The last part of the explanation should say what follows, and it is not that a reader has been deceived, since the system did what it was built to do; the reader has mistaken a measure of their own attention for a measure of what is out there, and the correction is to introduce material deliberately, from a source that did not choose them.

questions.explanation: The wording of an explanation like this matters, because the two easy versions are both wrong: the reader has not been lied to and the reader is not powerless. A system doing exactly what it was built to do is not a conspiracy, and a reader who believes otherwise will look for a villain and find none. The second error is the belief that changing a setting will restore a full range, since the bubble is drawn from behaviour and will be rebuilt. What an explanation has to hand the learner is a practical counter, and there is only one that works: choosing sources on purpose rather than accepting a sequence that was assembled out of their own reactions.

questions.topic: What a fact-check does and does not settle

It does not say that the opposite is true, because a false claim has an opposite and the two are not the same thing, and a reader who replaces one with the other has not checked anything so much as swapped errors. Nor does it say that nobody believes the claim, since belief and truth came apart long before any fact-checker arrived and are quite capable of coming apart again. What a good check gives is a reason: the record that was looked for, the date it was made, and the absence that was found instead. The reading error to name is the one where a verdict is treated as a closing door, so a reader meets a story that has been checked, finds it dull, and settles on an unchecked one that is at least lively. The correction is small and it is the same as for any evidence: a check is a piece of work to look at, not a verdict to inherit.

A learner who has been shown that a false claim does not establish its opposite is usually able to apply the correction at once, because the logical gap is visible; a learner who has only been told that some things are false has learned nothing they can use. questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Why a loanword is evidence of contact
questions.learningObjective: explain what a recorded loanword proves and what it does not
questions.stem: Explain why a word with a recorded foreign origin is evidence that two peoples were in contact, and say what it is not evidence of.

answer.exemplar: A loanword is a word that arrived, and a word cannot arrive without somebody carrying it. Huracán reached Spanish because speakers met a storm they had no word for, heard the word used for it and carried the sound home, and the word travelled more durably than the occasion did, which is why it is still in use and the voyage is forgotten. That makes loanwords among the most reliable traces a language leaves of its history, more reliable than a legend, because the word is in the evidence and can be dated. What it is not evidence of is a shortage in the language it came from: the languages of the Caribbean had a large vocabulary of their own, and a word travels because a thing travelled or a contact was useful, not because its speakers had run out. It is also not evidence of a direction of civilisation, and a claim that a people had no words for the sea because the sea went unnamed in another tongue is a claim about a record, not about a people.

questions.explanation: Two errors come out of this material and an explanation should name both, because both are common and neither is silly. The first is reading a loan as a deficiency in the source language, which turns a record of contact into a ranking of languages, and the second is reading it as a borrowing of civilisation rather than of a word. The reason the word is worth trusting as evidence is the point that does the work, and it should be stated plainly: the word is in the writing, the writing is dated, and a date is harder to argue with than a story. Everything else the item asks for follows from that one fact.

Stage two: the post leaves out the year the price last rose, the company that runs the service, and the evidence for the promise, and it leaves all three to the reader. That is the trade the format makes: a claim fits in fifteen words, and the conditions that would let a reader judge it do not. It also leaves out the author, since a post carries an account rather than a name, and a claim with an account behind it is one a reader cannot easily check. A stronger post would use the words for what can be verified and drop the rest, so a reader who wants to know can ask in the replies. The habit worth teaching is to ask after every short post who is left holding the claim, since that is the question the format is built to make you skip.

questions.explanation: The two stages are set so that the first cannot be completed well without noticing the second, and a learner asked only for the first will write a fluent post and think the task done. The brevity here is a real constraint rather than a game, and the point to draw out is that a short post is not a summary of a long one: it is a different object, built to be carried, and the material that does not carry is left behind by design. The second stage is also the transferable one, because the question of who is left holding a claim applies to any short form, and it is the question a reader should ask before repeating anything.
questions.hint: Ask who would have to be asked, after reading your post, before it could be believed.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Rewriting a headline and naming what it foregrounds
questions.learningObjective: change what a headline emphasises and state the new emphasis
questions.stem: Stage one: rewrite the headline 'Cae un porcentaje de Visitors en el pueblo' so that it foregrounds the cause rather than the figure. Stage two: say what your new headline now makes the reader expect to find.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: La sequía deja sin visitantes a la mitad de los pueblos de la comarca. Stage two: the new headline makes a reader expect a piece about a drought, so the cause has to be in the text or the headline will send people to a story that does not match what they were promised. That is the constraint a rewrite has to respect, and it is worth making a learner state it before the rewrite rather than after: a headline is a contract with the reader, and the contract is about what the text will contain. The other thing the rewrite changes is the scale, since a figure about visitors is now a drought affecting several places, which raises the stakes and makes the piece easier to share, which is exactly why the rewrite should be made deliberately rather than by habit.

questions.explanation: The two stages are in this order for a reason: a learner who rewrites first will usually produce something more dramatic rather than something differently pointed, because the pull in a headline is towards the stronger claim. Naming the new expectation forces the rewrite to be an act of construction, and it exposes the second thing a headline does, which is to promise a category of explanation. The last part is the one to draw out for a class, since a headline rewritten for reach is a small version of a claim made for an audience, and the discipline is the same in both.
questions.hint: Before you rewrite, decide what the reader will expect to find once they have read it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Explaining how a meme transmits and what it needs
questions.learningObjective: explain a form's transmission and name the condition it depends on
questions.stem: Stage one: explain in Spanish how a meme travels and what it needs in order to arrive intact. Stage two: name the one condition without which it does not arrive at all.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Un meme es un texto breve pegado a una imagen, y el texto solo no significa nada: señala algo que la imagen dice y que el lector tiene que ver para entenderlo. Por eso viaja en dos maneras, y en una llega entero y en la otra llega roto. Si se comparte la imagen con el texto, el efecto se conserva; si se copia solo el texto, queda la flecha sin aquello que señalaba. Stage two: the condition is that the reader has the image, or has the reference the image stands for. Without one of the two, the caption is a set of words with nothing to point at, and a reader either misses the point or supplies a meaning of their own, which is how a joke turns into a complaint. The second stage is worth pressing, because a learner will usually answer with a condition about the platform rather than one about the reader, and the platform is not what decides whether the thing arrives whole.

questions.explanation: The two stages separate two things learners blur together. The first is the mechanism, and it is worth setting out as a contrast between the routes rather than as a description of the form, because a description does not tell a reader why some shares work and some do not. The second is the condition, and pressing for it is the point of the item, since the answer is about the reader and not about the technology, and a learner who answers about the platform has not yet understood that the failure happens after the share. The last part is the practical consequence, and it is that a caption lifted out of its picture should not be repeated at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the caption points at, and what the reader must be holding when they arrive.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Two regional things and what makes each regional
questions.learningObjective: describe a regional dish and a genre, and name the shared marker of regionality
questions.stem: Stage one: describe a regional dish and a regional musical genre in two Spanish sentences each, using the marker of region rather than a list. Stage two: say what the two have in common that a work from a capital city does not.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: El mole negro de Oaxaca se hace con chile y chocolate, y lleva horas de cocer a fuego lento. El tango nació en Buenos Aires y en Montevideo, en los conventillos de la clase obrera. Stage two: what the two share is that each grew out of one place and one set of conditions, and a reader can name both. A dish built around chillies and cocoa is a dish of central and southern Mexico, and a dance music born in the tenements of the river cities belongs to the working people who danced it, and neither fact is a matter of opinion. A work made in a capital tends to circulate more widely and to lose its locality on the way, which is a reason for asking where a form came from and not only when, since a capital is a distribution point rather than a source. That question is the transferable one, and it works for a song, a dish and a novelist equally well.

questions.explanation: The two stages ask for the same discipline applied to two unrelated things, which is the point of pairing them: regionality is a property of origin, and it shows up in an ingredient list and in a sound without any connection between them. A learner asked only for the first will produce a list, and a list is the failure of the exercise, because a list of ingredients is exactly what a reader can find anywhere. The second stage is where the transfer happens, since a reader who has asked where a thing came from in two registers can ask it about the next thing without being reminded, and that is the habit the item is for.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can identify about the place, in each case, that a list would not tell them.
